  }}|image=Brice_Bosnich.jpg}}'''Brice Michael Bosnich''' {{post-nominals|country=AUS|FRS}}<ref name=frs/> (3 June 1936 – 13 April 2015)<ref>{{cite web|author=Anon|year=2015|url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/fellowship/notices-2015/|title=Notices 2015|publisher=royalsociety.org|location=London}}</ref> was an Australian [[inorganic chemist]].  He gained recognition for the design of complex ligands useful in [[homogeneous catalysis]].<ref name=boz>{{cite journal|last1=Crowley|first1=James D.|last2=Jackson|first2=W. Gregory|last3=Wild|first3=S. Bruce|title=Professor Brice Bosnich, FRS (1936–2015)|journal=Australian Journal of Chemistry|volume=69|issue=5|year=2016|pages=485|doi=10.1071/CHv69n5_FO|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Education==
He graduated from [[University of Sydney]] with a Bachelor of Science degree in 1958, and from [[Australian National University]] with a PhD in 1962, where he studied with [[Francis Patrick Dwyer]].<ref name=boz/> Contemporaries included [[Alan Sargeson]].<ref name=sargo>{{Cite journal | last1 = Bosnich | first1 = B. | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.2011.0017 | title = Alan McLeod Sargeson FAA. 13 October 1930 -- 29 December 2008 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 58 | pages = 265–282 | year = 2011 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=BosnichDwyer1960>{{cite journal|last1=Bosnich|first1=B.|last2=Dwyer|first2=F. P.|last3=Sargeson|first3=A. M.|title=Rate of Ligand Exchange with its Metal Complex by a Polarimetric Method|journal=Nature|volume=186|issue=4729|year=1960|pages=966|doi=10.1038/186966a0|bibcode=1960Natur.186..966B|s2cid=4224326|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=Bosnich1962>{{cite journal|last1=Bosnich|first1=B.|title=Bimolecular Substitution in Octahedral Transition Metal Ions, and the Concept of Amphiphilicity|journal=Nature|volume=196|issue=4860|year=1962|pages=1196–1197|doi=10.1038/1961196a0|bibcode=1962Natur.196.1196B|s2cid=4266781}}</ref>

==Career and research==
After leaving ANU, he taught at [[University College London]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.chem.ucl.ac.uk/resources/history/people/bosnich.html|title=The UCL Periodic Table of the Lecturers: Brice Bosnich|publisher=University College London}}</ref> He then moved to the [[University of Toronto]], where he remained from 1970 to 1987.  Thereafter he became Gustavus F. and Ann M. Swift Distinguished Service Professor at [[University of Chicago]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://chemistry.uchicago.edu/faculty/faculty/person/member/brice-bosnich.html|title=Chemistry Department – University of Chicago|work=uchicago.edu}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://chronicle.uchicago.edu/040122/dsp.shtml|title=Faculty receive named, distinguished appointments|work=uchicago.edu}}</ref> After his retirement he became a visiting fellow at his alma mater, [[Australian National University]].<ref name=boz/>

As an independent scientist at the University of Toronto, he developed a rational approach to chiral [[diphosphine]] ligands, the premier member being [[chiraphos]].  Unlike previous chiral ligands, the chirality of chiraphos arose from the backbone of the chelate.  This concept underpins many of the C2-symmetrical ligands subsequently developed in [[asymmetric hydrogenation]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Fryzuk | first1 = M. D. | last2 = Bosnich | first2 = B. | year = 1977 | title = Asymmetric synthesis. Production of optically active amino acids by catalytic hydrogenation | journal = J. Am. Chem. Soc. | volume = 99 | issue = 19 | pages = 6262–6267 | doi = 10.1021/ja00461a014 | pmid=893889| bibcode = 1977JAChS..99.6262F }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Fryzuk | first1 = M. D. | last2 = Bosnich | first2 = B. | year = 1978 | title = Asymmetric synthesis. An asymmetric homogeneous hydrogenation catalyst which breeds its own chirality | journal = J. Am. Chem. Soc. | volume = 100 | issue = 17 | pages = 5491–5494 | doi = 10.1021/ja00485a037 | bibcode = 1978JAChS.100.5491F }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Fryzuk | first1 = M. D. | last2 = Bosnich | first2 = B. | year = 1979 | title = Asymmetric synthesis. Preparation of chiral methyl chiral lactic acid by catalytic asymmetric hydrogenation | journal = J. Am. Chem. Soc. | volume = 101 | issue = 11 | pages = 3043–3049 | doi = 10.1021/ja00505a035 | bibcode = 1979JAChS.101.3043F }}</ref> Other areas of research included [[hydroacylation]] catalysis and the development of ligands that mimic the spectroscopic properties of the [[blue copper protein]]s.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Amundsen | first1 = Alan R. | last2 = Whelan | first2 = John | last3 = Bosnich | first3 = B. | year = 1977 | title = Biological analogs. Nature of the binding sites of copper-containing proteins | journal = J. Am. Chem. Soc. | volume = 99 | issue = 20| pages = 6730–6739 | doi = 10.1021/ja00462a042 | pmid = 893902 | bibcode = 1977JAChS..99.6730A }}</ref>

After his retirement, Bosnich [[climate change denial|questioned]] the [[Royal Society]]'s position on [[climate change]], which is the [[scientific consensus on climate change|scientific consensus on the subject]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Brice Bosnich. 3 June 1936—13 April 2015|year=2019 |publisher=The Royal Society|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2019.0019 |last1=Bennett |first1=Martin A. |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |volume=67 |pages=59–87 |s2cid=202401571 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
Bosnich was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 2000|Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) in 2000]].<ref name=frs>{{cite web|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160620151645/https://royalsociety.org/people/brice-bosnich-11117/ |archivedate=2016-06-20 |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/brice-bosnich-11117/ |publisher=royalsociety.org |location=London |title=Professor Brice Bosnich FRS }} One or more of the preceding sentences incorporates text from the royalsociety.org website where: {{quote|"All text published under the heading 'Biography' on Fellow profile pages is available under [[Creative Commons license|Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License]]." --{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |title=Royal Society Terms, conditions and policies |accessdate=2016-03-09 |url-status=bot: unknown |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925220834/https://royalsociety.org/about-us/terms-conditions-policies/ |archivedate=2015-09-25 }}}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bennett|first=Martin A.|date=2019|title=Brice Bosnich. 3 June 1936—13 April 2015|journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|volume=67|pages=59–87|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2019.0019|doi-access=free}}</ref> His biography reads: {{centred pull quote|Bosnich made many important contributions to inorganic and [[organometallic chemistry]]. A central theme of much of his research had been the [[stereochemistry]] of inorganic and organometallic complexes and of reactions mediated by such complexes. His design, synthesis and studies of the ligands, chiraphos and prophos, represent a major accomplishment and have contributed enormously to our understanding of the mechanisms of chiral recognition and asymmetric catalysis. Before his death, his research interests expanded to encompass the mechanistic aspects of a wide range of reactions, including allylic alkylations, metal catalysed [[Claisen rearrangement]]s, hydroacylation and [[hydrosilation]], as well as cooperative phenomena in binuclear metal complexes.<ref name=frs/>}}
